item.title: What We May Become: Why Psychosynthesis Still Matters
item.description:
Psychology

What We May Become: Why Psychosynthesis Still Matters

A century-old psychology asks a modern question: Who are we becoming?

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Psychosynthesis asks what becomes possible beyond symptom relief and compelling diagnostic narratives.
  • We can experience our inner dimensions and many aspects of self without allowing them to define us.
  • Psychological freedom begins when we consciously participate in who we are becoming.
Source: Photo: Roberto Assagioli; public domain, copyright cleared from WikiMedia Commons

We live in an age preoccupied with the question of who we are, yet uncertain about what to do with the answer.

Across this site and the wider psychological landscape, we are encouraged to construct identities, curate personalities, optimize ourselves, understand our wounds, regulate our nervous systems, and become the best possible version of ourselves. Yet beneath these differing perspectives lies a more difficult question:

What might we become?

This is one of the questions that makes psychosynthesis, a psychology developed by the Italian psychiatrist Roberto Assagioli, surprisingly relevant to modern life. Piero Ferrucci’s What We May Be offers one of its clearest and most accessible expressions—a vision of psychology concerned not only with repairing what has gone wrong, but with discovering what might emerge when the many dimensions of a person begin to work together.

Much of contemporary psychology has necessarily focused on suffering. We ask how depression develops, how trauma affects the nervous system, how anxiety can be managed, or how early childhood attachment patterns influence relationships. All are important, but once suffering has been understood and treatment attempted, what then?

Where do I begin in the present?

Psychosynthesis answers this question by beginning in the now.

Assagioli proposed that human beings are not merely collections of symptoms, diagnoses, memories, drives, or societal conditioning. We contain multiplicities: conflicting desires, roles, fears, ambitions, wounds, values, and aspirations. Psychosynthesis does not require us to eliminate these aspects of ourselves. Instead, it invites us to become aware of them without becoming completely identified with any one of them.

This process of dis-identification creates psychological space—a place from which we can observe ourselves and enter into a deeper relationship with our experience rather than simply reacting to it.

In some respects, modern psychotherapy is rediscovering something psychosynthesis was already exploring more than a century ago. Assagioli was exploring subpersonalities and disidentification decades before ‘parts work’ became popularized in therapy culture. Yet psychosynthesis did not stop at identifying our different parts; it situated them within a larger vision of consciousness and human development, reaching toward what would later become known as transpersonal psychology.

This may be one of the most useful ideas for our current historical moment, as many of us become overly identified with the stories we tell about ourselves: I am anxious; I am an extrovert; I am traumatized; I am successful; I am damaged; or, I am this political identity, that professional identity, this attachment style, or that diagnosis.

These experiences and descriptions can be illuminating when we are able to name and identify something, but they can also become narrative prisons that are far too reductive.

There is a profound difference between saying I experience anxiety and I am an anxious person. The first leaves room for fluid expression and psycho-somatic movement. The second can quickly become a rigid identity.

Psychosynthesis asks us to consider what becomes possible when we can hold our psychological experiences without allowing them to define the entirety of who we are. Ferrucci’s vision does not ask us to replace our ‘negative’ parts with happier or more functional ones but asks whether conflicting dimensions of ourselves might eventually become part of a larger whole.

Source: Jonny Gios / Unsplash

Bridging psychology and spirituality

For psychosynthesis, the human being possesses capacities that are not easily explained by pathology alone: intuition, creativity, compassion, beauty, love, meaning, and an impulse toward greater spiritual wholeness. These experiences need not be interpreted dogmatically or religiously; they can simply be taken as dimensions of human life.

In his book, Ferrucci describes this movement toward psychological and spiritual growth as something practical rather than merely theoretical, emphasizing techniques and practices that cultivate attention, freedom, will, and awareness.

Perhaps this is precisely what modern psychology and therapy culture needs: a broader conception of what healing is for.

A person who has learned to reduce their anxiety has accomplished something important, but what will they do with the freedom that anxiety management creates? A person who has worked through childhood wounds may finally experience greater stability, but what kind of life will they build from that stability?

Many therapies can help us integrate our past effectively. Psychosynthesis and related transpersonal psychotherapies can also help us become more available to our present and future.

So the question is not simply Who are you? but Who are you becoming?

There is something hopeful in this question. It assumes the psyche is not finished and leans into the dynamic, growth-oriented nature of our organism. For clinicians, this matters because healing is not always a return to a previous state of functioning. Sometimes healing is a reorganization—an authentic synthesis—through which a person becomes capable of living from a larger sense of wholeness. Of course, not every wound has a purpose or every loss a redemption, but we may still choose how we relate to what cannot be changed.

Psychosynthesis places considerable emphasis on our centre of consciousness, and our capacity to choose, direct attention, and actively participate in our own lives. In an age of algorithms, distractions, polarization, and increasingly sophisticated forms of persuasion, that may be more radical than it sounds.

Perhaps psychological freedom is not the absence of influence, but the ability to notice what is influencing us and decide, with increasing consciousness, what deserves our allegiance. That may be a question worth bringing into modern psychotherapy discourse: What in me is waiting to become?

item.title: Resilience Is the Dolly Parton Way
item.description:
Resilience

Resilience Is the Dolly Parton Way

How Parton reframed adversity and fueled her legendary life and career.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Adversity can be a journey of hope. A positive mindset can turn the impossible into something possible.
  • Experiencing lows in life is a normal part of being human.
  • Instead of seeing hardship as a dead end, we can pivot to find a better option.
Source: Adam Shanker on Shutterstock

Dolly Parton, who died yesterday at age 80, was famous for her music and for her dogged resilience. The odds seemed to be against her from the start, but she overcame many obstacles. Raised in rural poverty, Parton transcended her circumstances and became a successful female artist in a male-dominated industry.

Throughout her life, she responded to adversity by reframing negative experiences into positivity that fueled momentum. Her mindset was one of her greatest tools. Here are some of her most famous beliefs and sayings, lessons that can help us all grapple with hard times:

"If you don't like the road you're walking, start paving another one.” We don’t have to feel stuck in life. We can pivot to a new opportunity. We can shift our perspective; instead of seeing a dead end, we can view an untenable situation as a fork in the road.

“The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you've got to put up with the rain!" Dolly reframed adversity as a journey of hope. Adversity is a prerequisite for resilience. Reaching a goal requires moving through obstacles and difficult times. Science agrees. Research from New York University shows how confronting and moving through realistic obstacles can help a person achieve their goals.

“Storms make trees take deeper roots.” We might feel battered during difficult times. Yet, in her view, difficult times make us better. Rather than diminishing or defeating us, bad times can empower us and strengthen our inner character. Research on post-traumatic growth shows how a life crisis can force positive transformation and deep inner strength.

“Anyone who says you can’t take it with you has never seen me pack.” Self-confidence, resourcefulness, creativity, and a positive mindset can turn the impossible into the possible. We each have agency. And we find out that external limits can be flexible. When you change how you think and act, tough problems are solvable. With a growth mindset, hard limits are just temporary skills waiting to be learned.

“We cannot direct the wind, but we can adjust the sails.” While we can't change what is beyond our control, we can adapt and turn a negative into a positive. We can not only survive a challenge but thrive. Therapies like acceptance and commitment show us we can learn to stop fighting difficult situations, be psychologically flexible, and start adapting.

“If you’re feeling low, don’t despair. The sun has a sinking spell every night, but it comes back up every morning.” The antidote to hopelessness is hope. Yet, no matter how positive we may be, we are human. We all experience lows, but it’s important to remember that we’ll always rise again. The late psychologist John Cacioppo likely agrees; he researched how we can expect good things to happen.

That's doggedness.

In the words of Dolly Parton, “You can’t just sit around and think of all the things you want to do. You’ve got to think of what you want to do, and then you’ve got to get out and make that happen.” Stay dogged.

item.title: Can the Use of AI Chatbots Be Compulsive?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Can the Use of AI Chatbots Be Compulsive?

Teenagers are worried about their reliance on AI chatbots.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Many teenagers report that they are concerned about their relationships with AI chatbots.
  • A reliance on chatbots hinders teens’ abilities to learn how to gain crucial social skills.
  • That reliance on chatbots makes their usefulness in addiction treatment suspect.

There are times when we just want to vent and have others mirror our thoughts and emotions. This may be especially true for teenagers who are in the midst of significant and challenging stages of physical, psychological, and social development. They and their worlds change so quickly, which can be very disorienting. Could AI chatbots provide some needed help? Does it come with a price?

AI chatbots for teen support

A recent study from Drexel University finds that teens ages 13-17 are becoming concerned with their relationships with AI chatbots. More teens are turning to chatbots for emotional support, connection, and companionship. While some of the teens used these chatbots in relatively harmless ways, others reported that the connections become stronger and feel very difficult to break.

Analyzing more than 300 posts on Reddit from teens about their interactions, researchers “were able to see clear patterns like conflict, withdrawal, and relapse showing up in their posts, which suggests this is more than just frequent or enthusiastic use.” The researchers found evidence of six of the features of behavioral addictions (gambling, for example) that were reported by the teens. These include strongly conflicting desires about continuing to use or engage with the chatbots, salience or a deepening connection, tolerance, withdrawal, relapse, and mood regulation or dysregulation.

AI was designed to increase and enhance users’ experiences. Agreement, flattery, and affirmation are time-tested ways to draw people out; AI has just supercharged those methods. Since AI mirrors input so well, its responses may be terribly skewed. In many ways, AI chatbots may be telling us exactly what we want to hear even if we do not recognize this.

Imagine having a deep disagreement with a friend whom you feel has wronged you terribly. You convey your side of the story, offering excruciating detail of every grievance to the chatbot. In many ways, the chatbot seems the perfect sounding board, offering a sympathetic ear equivalent and not pushing back in any significant way.

Is near-total agreement the perfect sounding board? In an age of AI chatbots, many young people may assume this is what it means to be supportive. But is it? No doubt there are times when agreement and affirmation are appropriate and therefore supportive. However, there are times when being supportive means respectfully disagreeing, pushing back, and slowing someone’s roll.

Part of maturing is learning how to go to particular people when you need advice. We need to learn how to discern who is a good sounding board and source of wisdom. We sometimes seek the person who will tell us something we don’t necessarily want to hear but know we must. We need someone who respects us and has our best interests at heart. We don’t need bootlickers, toadies, or brown-nosers.

article continues after advertisement

As we grow older, we also learn how to identify and ask for what we need when seeking someone with whom to share confidences and solicit advice. Sometimes we may just need to vent, while at other times we need to problem-solve. This awareness of what we need is a crucial dimension of self-knowledge.

Engagement and conversation are arts, learned most often by direct and in-person interactions. In the age of AI, when young people seek support and advice, they will lack opportunities to develop other vital skills, such as learning to question others and themselves, arguing for their positions, and revising their own perspectives.

AI in addiction treatment

Complicating the issue is that AI is being incorporated into addiction treatment. Something to which people may become dependent is now a component of addiction treatment. This presents profound questions and challenges, especially for younger people who have not fully developed those skills and arts of seeking advice.

AI has some roles to play in addiction treatment and recovery. AI can answer questions about the various effects that addictive substances and behaviors have on brains, social relations, workplace productivity, and avenues for treatment and recovery. With guardrails and effective supervision, AI may play an effective interactive role.

The concerns about mirroring and reflecting producing skewed recommendations burn brightly, though, especially with younger people. Those who are already worried about their dependence on AI chatbots and those who worry about their gambling, drinking, or use of other substances may still turn to AI. It is convenient and accessible, unlike most in-person treatment and recovery options. That needs to change.

item.title: When Strong Self-Reliance Becomes Emotional Isolation
item.description:
Relationships

When Strong Self-Reliance Becomes Emotional Isolation

The hidden cost of never letting anyone see you struggle

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Self-reliance can become isolation when you never let others see that you need help.
  • Vulnerability isn't weakness or oversharing; it's choosing when, how, and whom to trust.
  • Fear of burdening others can create distance from the important people in your life.
  • Start small: naming your feelings and sharing them can help others become closer to you.

Not many people would willingly describe themselves as vulnerable. It’s unpleasant to imagine being unprotected and susceptible to pain.

But have you ever felt as though something was really bothering you, yet you didn’t want to talk about it? Have you felt annoyed when someone asked you “What’s wrong?” Have you ever regretted disclosing something personal immediately after you’ve said it? Or maybe it’s easy for you to describe your circumstances, but not at all easy to say “I’m scared,” or “That really hurts,” or “I really need a friend right now.” All of these examples describe the fear of vulnerability in action, in ways that most of us can probably relate to.

Source: Image created by ChatGPT / AI-Generated

Those who aren’t comfortable with vulnerability may be proud of the way they handle their own problems (even when they look overwhelming). They don’t want to burden their friends, partners, or family members—or maybe they just don’t like talking about their own feelings but can easily be emotionally articulate about other people. It’s just that when someone asks what they need, or what they’re feeling, things seem different.

The goal may be self-reliance—never letting anyone else see you struggle—but sometimes, the habits that help you rely on yourself when things get tough can limit your ability to form and deepen relationships. There’s a big difference between bearing up against adversity and isolating yourself from connection to others.

Being vulnerable means allowing another person to know something personal about you—something that matters, but might also feel like a risk, because once you let it out, you won’t be able to control the other person’s response. (It’s not the same as oversharing, breaking down in tears, or being weak.) Being vulnerable could mean telling another person that you’re worried about something, that you don’t know what to do, or that you’re afraid they might be angry at you. It could even be admitting that you really want a relationship to work, or that you need help.

This isn’t equivalent to emotional dumping, and it doesn’t mean telling the other person everything. While there’s no predetermined way to “do it right,” healthy vulnerability is selective: It involves making good judgments about whom to trust, what to tell them, and when you choose to say it.

This can be particularly difficult for men these days. The stereotypical masculine norm emphasizes self-reliance, emotional control, independent achievement, and “toughness”—qualities that advertising executives played up when they created the “Marlboro Man” decades ago. These culture-permeating ideas can make it hard for men to feel comfortable with emotional vulnerability, even when it could be good for them.

A 2025 meta-analysis by Emir Üzümçeker—a psychology professor at Dokuz Eylül University in Izmir, Turkey—found that traditional masculinity was associated with negative attitudes toward seeking help from others. Yet in 2024, a study by Choi and Sabey in a journal called Psychology of Men & Masculinities found that while men’s group participants were aware of these traditionally stoic, isolating expectations, they also knew that real strength could develop from talking about their problems and being understood. In other words, while many men seem to be absorbing the message that competence is the same as self-sufficiency, it’s also possible for them to reconcile that sense of competence with greater comfort in needing other people.

Accordingly, holding back from vulnerability can come with a relational cost. A partner can easily misinterpret the fear of vulnerability as emotional withholding—as rejection, indifference, or a lack of trust—even if the withholding partner is only trying not to “burden” the other. And for someone without a long-term partner, vulnerability can make it more difficult to find one.

It helps us form emotional bonds with others, be they colleagues at work, people we know from the bar, or other people on a team. Even old friends can end up just “coasting” on their history, skimming the surface of their friendship, if they’re no longer accustomed to diving in more deeply. It’s surprisingly easy to find yourself with a busy life, crowded with people, yet without anyone to call when something goes wrong. When we consistently prevent other people from seeing our needs and fears, we create obstacles to genuine intimacy. It’s a paradox: avoiding vulnerability is something we do to protect ourselves from the pain of rejection, but really, it only does so by making it impossible for anyone to get close enough to reject us.

Naturally, the goal isn’t to open the taps and to let all of your feelings out, all of the time; it’s to develop the habit of becoming discriminating about vulnerability—of choosing the right people to earn your trust. In a study of over 1,000 American adults, Epstein, Newland & Reid (2025) concluded that real emotional bonds are created when one person’s vulnerability is met with another person’s empathy. Reciprocating vulnerability, they suggest, creates stronger connections, even among men, many of whose friendships are less deep than they once were.

If you’re wondering what you can do about this, don’t stress: you can start small. Try to notice what you do when someone asks you how you are, and you’re not feeling your best. Do you joke, or change the subject, or try to “solve the problem”? Is there any more room to describe your feelings, at least a little, before you do that?

To yourself, try out a few words for what you’re going through: Are you “worried,” “hurt,” or “lonely”? If it’s difficult to do that, maybe you need a bit of practice with emotional labeling first. You can try it when you watch a movie or TV show: How would you describe what the character is feeling? What specific reaction is the actor trying to convey? The more you ask yourself this question, the better your emotional vocabulary, and the easier it can be to find words for your own emotions.

If you think you may have isolated yourself in this way, don’t wait for an emergency before you take action. Create a chance to talk to someone you know. You can start by asking for something specific; maybe you’d just like someone to listen to you, and you don’t need advice. Maybe you have a decision to make, and it could help to talk through your options out loud.

Either way, once you’ve taken the initiative to disclose, try not to retreat. Let the other person respond, and listen to what they say to you. They may be open about their own feelings and let you know they care about you; even if it is uncomfortable, try to sit with it long enough to take it in. Be open to whatever results from your effort, too. The attempt to express your feelings might turn out to be safer than you expected it to be.

One might even say that being vulnerable with other people is about them as much as it is about you: It means you’ve allowed them to matter to you, enough to help you carry whatever it is you’re struggling with. And, as the research suggests, even as this process helps them become more important to you, you’ll become more important to them, too.
